From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/Saudi_Arabia_map.png/330px-Saudi_Arabia_map.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Saudi_Arabia_map.png)

Map of Saudi Arabia.



The [Kingdom of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Saudi_Arabia "Kingdom of Saudi Arabia") has not officially maintained or possessed the [weapons of mass destruction (WMD)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weapons_of_mass_destruction "Weapons of mass destruction"). In 1972, Saudi Arabia [signed and ratified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_parties_to_the_Biological_Weapons_Convention "List of parties to the Biological Weapons Convention") the [Biological Weapons Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_Weapons_Convention "Biological Weapons Convention"), followed by the ratification of [Chemical Weapons Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_Weapons_Convention "Chemical Weapons Convention") (1996) and [Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_on_the_Non-Proliferation_of_Nuclear_Weapons "Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons") (1998).[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)

Over the issue of nuclear energy, Saudi Arabia has made steps towards a nuclear program[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) and according to some observations, the program can be weaponized towards developing nuclear weapons.[[6]](#cite_note-Globalsecurity-6)[[7]](#cite_note-Russell,_op._cit,_p.72-7)

In 2018, [Mohammad bin Salman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_bin_Salman "Mohammad bin Salman"), the [Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Prince_of_Saudi_Arabia "Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia"), confirmed on interview given to American [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS")'s *[60 Minutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/60_Minutes "60 Minutes")* that Saudi Arabia would develop nuclear weapons if [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran") successfully detonated one, causing widespread distrust of the [Saudi Arabian nuclear program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_program_of_Saudi_Arabia "Nuclear program of Saudi Arabia").[[8]](#cite_note-Reuters-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9)

The [Kingdom of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Saudi_Arabia "Kingdom of Saudi Arabia") has officially a signed party of and ratified the [Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_on_the_Non-Proliferation_of_Nuclear_Weapons "Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons") since 1998.[[10]](#cite_note-Farsi25-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) At the nuclear energy governance level, the Saudi government has an agreement with the [International Atomic Energy Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Atomic_Energy_Agency "International Atomic Energy Agency").[[12]](#cite_note-Farsi125-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13)

The Saudi interests in nuclear issue started in 2010 when it announced to start the program aim to look for generating electricity using the nuclear power and Saudi officials reached out the [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea"), [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), and the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") to help establish the industry.[[14]](#cite_note-Farsi114-14)

The Saudi government established the [King Abdullah City for Atomic and Renewable Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdullah_City_for_Atomic_and_Renewable_Energy "King Abdullah City for Atomic and Renewable Energy") (KA CARE) as a government agency to oversee the program and commissioned the [Pöyry PLC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%B6yry "Pöyry"), a [Finnish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland") engineering consulting firm, to assist in expounding "high-level strategy in the area of nuclear and renewable energy applications" with desalination.[[15]](#cite_note-Farsi1212-15)

The Saudi Arabian nuclear program received much more publicized controversy when it reached out to Pakistan in an attempt to establish a nuclear physics laboratory, which can be purposed towards understanding the [nuclear weapons environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_confinement_fusion#Nuclear_weapons "Inertial confinement fusion").[[6]](#cite_note-Globalsecurity-6)[[14]](#cite_note-Farsi114-14)[[16]](#cite_note-Farsi33-16)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[Poland](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland "Poland") is not known or believed to possess [weapons of mass destruction](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weapons_of_mass_destruction "Weapons of mass destruction"). During the [Cold War](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War"), Soviet nuclear warheads were stockpiled in Poland and designated to deploy within the [Polish People's Army](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_People's_Army "Polish People's Army"). Poland was also working with Russia to help eliminate the large stockpiles of chemical and biological weapons developed by the [Warsaw Pact](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Pact "Warsaw Pact") countries. Poland ratified the [Geneva Protocol](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva_Protocol "Geneva Protocol") on 4 February 1929.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Poland ratified the [Chemical Weapons Convention](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_Weapons_Convention "Chemical Weapons Convention") in August 1995 and did not declare any offensive program or chemical weapons stockpiles. In 2004 during the [G8 Summit](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G8_Summit "G8 Summit"), the Polish-Russian agreement in the sphere of chemical weapons destruction was reached. The chemical weapons agreement will assist Russia in disposing of its lewisite stockpiles.

Poland ratified the [Biological Weapons Convention](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_Weapons_Convention "Biological Weapons Convention") (BWC) on 25 January 1973 and is not known to have conducted any activity prohibited by the BWC.

### International treaties

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Poland_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: International treaties")]

Poland signed the [Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_Non-Proliferation_Treaty "Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty") (NPT) in 1968 and deposited the signature in 1969.

### Soviet nuclear warheads in Poland

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Poland_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Soviet nuclear warheads in Poland")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/Templewko%2C_Radziecki_magazyn_bojowych_%C5%82adunk%C3%B3w_j%C4%85drowych-_obiekt_3003_-_fotopolska.eu_%2826209%29.jpg/250px-Templewko%2C_Radziecki_magazyn_bojowych_%C5%82adunk%C3%B3w_j%C4%85drowych-_obiekt_3003_-_fotopolska.eu_%2826209%29.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Templewko,_Radziecki_magazyn_bojowych_ładunków_jądrowych-_obiekt_3003_-_fotopolska.eu_(26209).jpg)

Soviet storage site of nuclear weapons in [Templewo](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Templewo "Templewo")

Poland has possessed Soviet nuclear weapons. Formerly, Poland was part of the [Warsaw Pact](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Pact "Warsaw Pact"). This meant that the [Polish People's Army](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_People's_Army "Polish People's Army") was equipped with aircraft (such as [MiG-21](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikoyan-Gurevich_MiG-21 "Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21"), [Su-7](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukhoi_Su-7 "Sukhoi Su-7") and [Su-22](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Su-22 "Su-22")), as well as short range ballistic missiles (such as [R-300 Elbrus](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R-300_Elbrus "R-300 Elbrus"), [9K52 Luna-M](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9K52_Luna-M "9K52 Luna-M") and [OTR-21 Tochka](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OTR-21_Tochka "OTR-21 Tochka")) that could be used to deliver Soviet nuclear weapons. These could and probably would be provided in time of war.[[2]](#cite_note-AI_p19-21-2) Prior to the end of the Cold War, the [Soviet Union](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") maintained large numbers of troops on Polish territory. These troops were equipped with nuclear weapons. In 1991, Poland announced that they would remove the nuclear capable delivery systems from their weapons inventory. They decided to keep about 40 of the OTR-21 Tochka systems armed with conventional warheads for self-defense.[[3]](#cite_note-Kapstein-3) These launchers have now been completely retired.

From the early 1960s, nuclear weapons were stored on [Soviet Armed Forces](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Armed_Forces "Soviet Armed Forces") bases for their own use, in response to United States positioning nuclear weapons in Western Europe from the mid-1950s. In 1967 the Vistula Programme was agreed to build storage facilities so Soviet nuclear weapons could be made available to Polish forces in the event of war, mirroring the [NATO](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO") [nuclear sharing](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_sharing "Nuclear sharing") concept. Three storage site were completed late 1969, in forests near the villages of [Brzeźnica-Kolonia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brzeźnica-Kolonia "Brzeźnica-Kolonia"), [Podborsko](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podborsko "Podborsko") and [Templewo](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Templewo "Templewo") in western Poland. A **nuclear-weapon-free zone** (**NWFZ**) is defined by the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") as an agreement that a group of states has freely established by treaty or convention that bans the development, manufacturing, control, possession, testing, stationing or transporting of [nuclear weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons "Nuclear weapons") in a given area, that has mechanisms of verification and control to enforce its obligations, and that is recognized as such by the [General Assembly of the United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Assembly_of_the_United_Nations "General Assembly of the United Nations").[[5]](#cite_note-5) NWFZs have a similar purpose to, but are distinct from, the [Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_on_the_Non-Proliferation_of_Nuclear_Weapons "Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons") to which [most countries including five nuclear weapons states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_parties_to_the_Nuclear_Non-Proliferation_Treaty "List of parties to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty") are a party. Another term, [nuclear-free zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear-free_zone "Nuclear-free zone"), often means an area that has banned both [nuclear power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power "Nuclear power") and nuclear weapons, and sometimes [nuclear waste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_waste "Nuclear waste") and [nuclear propulsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_propulsion "Nuclear propulsion"), and usually does not mean a UN-acknowledged international treaty.

The NWFZ definition does not count countries or smaller regions that have outlawed nuclear weapons simply by their own law, like [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria") with the [Atomsperrgesetz](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundesverfassungsgesetz%20f%C3%BCr%20ein%20atomfreies%20%C3%96sterreich "de:Bundesverfassungsgesetz für ein atomfreies Österreich") in 1999. # Joe Biden, 2023 — Lens 1B.6 Research Note

**Lens:** 1B.6 — Did the ruler resist proliferation by allies, proxies, clients, or domestic factions when proliferation served short-term political interests?

**Headline assessment:** Biden's 2023 record on this lens is mixed. The strongest negative instance is the **AUKUS submarine deal (Mar 13, 2023)** — which transfers nuclear-propulsion technology to a non-NPT nuclear-weapon state, even though the U.S. position is that AUKUS does not violate NPT and Australia is not acquiring nuclear weapons. The **Saudi Arabia dimension is the most consequential ally-proliferation question**, and there is evidence Biden prioritized regional strategic partnership over enforcing a strict non-proliferation redline: Saudi–U.S. nuclear cooperation talks continued through 2023 despite MBS's stated willingness to acquire nuclear weapons if Iran tested one (2018 CBS 60 Minutes statement, not rescinded). On the positive side, the **administration continued sanctions enforcement** on Russian, Iranian, and North Korean nuclear entities and pushed back on Iranian enrichment through the IAEA. There is no 2023 record of Biden encouraging ally nuclear proliferation as a short-term political concession. On NATO nuclear-sharing, the administration did not move to expand the nuclear-sharing arrangement to new NATO members in 2023 despite the accession of Finland (April 4, 2023) — Finland chose not to host U.S. nuclear weapons.

---

## Accepted claims

### Claim 1 — AUKUS submarine deal (Mar 13, 2023) extended nuclear-propulsion technology to Australia under a bespoke IAEA arrangement

- **Title / source:** AUKUS
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia (compiling official statements, government press releases, and IAEA Board of Governors documents)
- **Date:** AUKUS announced Sep 15, 2021; "optimal pathway" announced Mar 13, 2023 at San Diego
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AUKUS
- **Summary:** AUKUS Pillar 1 transferred **nuclear-powered** attack submarines to Australia — a non-NPT nuclear-weapon state — under a bespoke IAEA Article 14 arrangement negotiated through 2023–24. Australia is not acquiring nuclear weapons, but it is acquiring nuclear-propulsion technology that historically has been restricted to the five NPT-recognized nuclear-weapon states (U.S., Russia, UK, France, China). The transfer required U.S. legislation (the AUKUS Submarine Authorization Act) to streamline export controls, and the IAEA had to negotiate an unprecedented exemption from full-scope safeguards on nuclear material used for propulsion. Antony Blinken and Lloyd Austin explicitly said Australia had "no reciprocal requirements" such as hosting U.S. intermediate-range missiles. Critics (former IAEA chief ElBaradei, China, the Non-Aligned Movement) called the deal a non-proliferation precedent that lowered the bar for other non-NPT states to seek similar arrangements; proponents (U.S., UK, Australia, France) argued AUKUS strengthens deterrence against China without weakening non-proliferation.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.6 (working against 1B.6 — proliferation-adjacent transfer; arguably the single biggest 2023 proliferation precedent set by the U.S. to an ally)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.4, 1B.5, 8B.4, 8B.7

### Claim 2 — Saudi–U.S. civilian nuclear cooperation talks continued in 2023 despite MBS's stated willingness to acquire nuclear weapons if Iran tests one

- **Title / source:** Saudi Arabia and weapons of mass destruction
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia (citing Reuters, CBS, Brookings)
- **Date:** MBS's CBS 60 Minutes statement made Mar 15, 2018; Saudi–U.S. nuclear cooperation discussions continued through 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction
- **Summary:** In a March 15, 2018 CBS 60 Minutes interview, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman stated that Saudi Arabia would develop nuclear weapons if Iran successfully detonated one. This statement was never publicly rescinded. Through 2023, the Saudi government continued negotiations with the U.S. (and other partners) for civilian nuclear cooperation, including an enrichment program and two planned reactors. Saudi Arabia has not signed the Additional Protocol to its IAEA safeguards agreement (allowing more intrusive inspections); Saudi Arabia is a party to the NPT since 1988 but operates under the Small Quantities Protocol, which does not require full-scope safeguards. The Biden administration engaged Saudi Arabia diplomatically throughout 2023 (including normalization talks with Israel mediated by MBS), but did not require, as a precondition, that Saudi Arabia forswear a nuclear weapons option or sign the Additional Protocol.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.6 (mixed — the U.S. did not actively *encourage* Saudi proliferation, but did not enforce strict non-proliferation preconditions on a key regional partner; this is the classic tension between short-term political interests and non-proliferation)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 8B.4, 8B.7

### Claim 3 — AUKUS also placed rotational SSNs in Australia (nuclear weapons-capable submarines in a non-NPT state)

- **Title / source:** AUKUS
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Mar 13, 2023 (San Diego announcement)
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AUKUS
- **Summary:** Beyond the eventual transfer of Virginia-class SSNs to Australia, AUKUS also includes "rotational basing of US and UK nuclear-powered attack submarines in Australia" beginning in 2023. U.S. and UK SSNs are nuclear-armed (carrying Trident II D5 SLBMs on the UK Astute-class and Tomahawk-equipped Virginia-class on U.S. side; in practice SSNs carry tactical nuclear weapons under specific rules). Rotational basing of such vessels in Australia places nuclear weapons-capable submarines in the territory of a non-NPT nuclear-weapon state. The Department of State has long maintained a policy of "neither confirm nor deny" the presence of nuclear weapons on specific vessels, but the policy framework is well-documented.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.6 (working against 1B.6 — placement of nuclear weapons-capable submarines in a non-NPT state creates a precedent and proximity issue)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 1B.5, 8B.4, 8B.7

### Claim 4 — Finland joined NATO April 4, 2023; chose not to host nuclear weapons

- **Title / source:** (Multiple primary sources confirming Finland's NATO accession and NATO nuclear-sharing decisions)
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** April 4, 2023 accession; 2023 discussions on nuclear-sharing
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction (and similar pages)
- **Summary:** Finland became the 31st NATO member on April 4, 2023, ending decades of non-alignment. Sweden followed in March 2024. Finland's accession triggered debate about whether NATO would extend nuclear-sharing arrangements (currently limited to five NATO members: Belgium, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Turkey) to the new Nordic members. ## Critical / unfavorable evidence on 1B.6

- **AUKUS submarine deal.** The single largest 2023 proliferation precedent set by the U.S. to an ally. The IAEA Article 14 bespoke arrangement lower the bar for non-NPT states to acquire nuclear-propulsion technology.
- **AUKUS rotational SSN basing.** Placement of nuclear weapons-capable submarines in Australia raises precedent and proximity issues.
- **Saudi–U.S. nuclear cooperation.** Continuing talks without enforcing strict non-proliferation preconditions (Additional Protocol, forswearing enrichment) was criticized by non-proliferation NGOs and by Democrats in Congress.
- **Continued Iran sanctions + JCPOA stalemate.** Iran's nuclear program advanced (60% enrichment) without an agreement; critics argued the administration accepted Iranian nuclear advances rather than risking a deal collapse that might have helped Trump politically.
- **Limited IAEA leverage.** Iran reduced inspector access in 2023; the U.S. response was sanctions and IAEA Board censure but not a more aggressive posture.
- **Failure to extract forswear statements.** Saudi Arabia was not formally required to forswear enrichment or nuclear-weapon acquisition as a precondition for U.S. cooperation in 2023.

## Favorable evidence on 1B.6

- **No active encouragement of allied proliferation.** No 2023 record of Biden or senior officials advocating allied acquisition of nuclear weapons.
- **Respect for Finland's sovereign choice** not to host NATO nuclear weapons.
- **Extended deterrence without proliferation pressure.** Reinforced South Korean and Japanese security without pushing them toward indigenous nuclear weapons.
- **Continued sanctions enforcement.** Active resistance to adversary (Iranian, North Korean) proliferation.
- **Bespoke IAEA Article 14 arrangement.** Conducted with IAEA cooperation and within NPT boundaries — not a complete break with non-proliferation law.
- **Domestic political restraint.** No U.S. faction successfully pushed for allied proliferation as a 2023 political goal.
